name: Satisfaction paradox
aliases: Paradox of the contented female worker
statement: Women report job satisfaction as high as or higher than men while holding jobs that pay less and offer less.
meaning: Two different findings travel under this name, and the entry has to pick one. In medicine the satisfaction paradox is Herschbach's observation that objectively negative circumstances have little effect on subjective quality of life, which the social sciences call the well-being paradox. This entry is about the other one, the labour-market finding usually called the paradox of the contented female worker. Its claim is narrower and easier to test. Women are paid less, promoted less and report more discrimination at work, and they still rate their jobs at least as highly as men rate theirs. The gap survives controls for the jobs people actually hold, so it is not produced by men and women doing different work. Andrew Clark's account is that satisfaction measures the distance between a job and what the worker expected of it, and that women expected less because women had held worse jobs in the past. That account carries a prediction. As women's position in the labour market improves and expectations converge on men's, the gap should shrink and then vanish.

origin.note: Crosby's book Relative Deprivation and Working Women gave the pattern its name. Clark's 1997 paper in Labour Economics established it in economics and supplied the expectations account, and Hodson had asked the same question in The Sociological Quarterly in 1989. The Crosby attribution is quoted from Brüggemann and Hinz, who write that the finding 'was termed the "paradox of the contented female worker" by Crosby (1982)'. The book itself was not obtained.

evidence: Clark's paper could not be obtained, so what it did is reported here from two later papers that use it. Vladisavljević and Perugini write that Clark grouped the candidate explanations into five sets, differences in individual and job characteristics, differences in work values, selection bias, differences in relative income distributions and differences in expectations, and found the first four insufficient. They also record his finding that no significant gender gap appeared among younger workers, highly educated workers, workers whose mothers had professional jobs, workers in professional or managerial posts, and workers in male-dominated workplaces. Green, Heywood, Kler and Leeves report Clark's adjusted 1991 gap as 0.240 satisfaction points. Later work does not agree on whether the pattern is still there. Vladisavljević and Perugini used the 2013 EU-SILC well-being module for 32 European countries, with job satisfaction on an eleven-point scale, and found a pooled female advantage of 0.058 points on a matched sample. The country-level picture is split. The female advantage reached significance in seven countries, Portugal, the United Kingdom, Iceland, Malta, the Netherlands, Cyprus and Hungary, while men were significantly more satisfied in Croatia, Bulgaria, Slovakia and Poland. Redmond and McGuinness used the 2014 European Skills and Jobs Survey, which covers 48,000 workers in 28 EU countries. A female advantage survived their personal, job and family controls. It disappeared once nine job preferences were added, with work-life balance and intrinsic interest doing most of the work. Brüggemann and Hinz turned the question to pay fairness, using round 9 of the European Social Survey from 2018. Their sample is 13,544 respondents in 752 occupations across 27 countries, each rating their own gross pay from extremely unfairly low to extremely unfairly high. Women rated their pay less fair than men, by 0.251 scale points raw and 0.139 with controls, and the raw coefficient ran that way in 23 of the 27 countries. Dilmaghani studied the Canadian General Social Survey for 2016. Her abstract reports a female advantage that holds in the aggregate and falls to insignificance among the youngest and most educated workers. Once subjective intrinsic rewards are controlled for it reverses in favour of men among holders of graduate degrees.

replication.headline: Clark's 1991 British estimate reproduces on his own data source, and the gap in that series is gone by 2012, while studies in other countries and on other measures disagree about whether it survives anywhere.
replication.detail: Green, Heywood, Kler and Leeves re-estimated Clark's specification on the British Household Panel Survey and its successor, Understanding Society, an unbalanced panel of 22,328 individuals running from 1991 to 2012. Job satisfaction is a seven-point scale. In 1991 the raw female advantage was 0.305 satisfaction points and the advantage adjusted for individual and job characteristics was 0.234, against the 0.240 they report from Clark. By 2008 the raw figure was 0.162 and the adjusted figure 0.100. By 2012 the raw figure was 0.023 and the adjusted figure 0.009, neither distinguishable from zero. Mean female satisfaction fell from about 5.7 in the early years to the 5.2 to 5.3 band that men occupied throughout. An Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition puts the whole of the 1991 raw difference of 0.401 in the coefficients rather than the characteristics, and puts the later decline there too: women's jobs did not get worse, women judged them more harshly. None of the yearly estimates from 2008 to 2012 differ from zero at the 5 per cent level. These figures are read from the 2016 Lancaster University Management School working paper, which is titled 'Paradox Lost: Disappearing Female Job Satisfaction'. The published article of 2018 was not obtained and its numbers were not checked against the working paper's.

study.cite: Green, C. P., Heywood, J. S., Kler, P., & Leeves, G. (2018). Paradox Lost: The Disappearing Female Job Satisfaction Premium. British Journal of Industrial Relations, 56(3), 484-502.

limits: Clark's paper was not obtained. ScienceDirect returned 403, Crossref carries no abstract for it, OpenAlex records it as closed with no repository copy, and searches of RePEc, IDEAS, the Kingston University research portal and open web indexes turned up only the citation. Every figure credited to Clark on this page is quoted from a paper that cites him, and none of it went into the structured fields. Green and colleagues state that their evidence uses Clark's original data source and is unique to the United Kingdom, and they decline to claim the trend extends beyond it. That caution matters because the pattern was reported most consistently in Anglo-Saxon countries. The studies gathered here are not repeats of one another. Overall job satisfaction, satisfaction with pay and the perceived fairness of one's own wage are three different measures, and only the British series re-estimates the original specification on the original data. The working paper by Vladisavljević and Perugini describes the sign of its own early-life gender-equality interaction in two directions. Its results section says the coefficient is negative, its table prints 0.465 and its conclusion says exposure to early equality is connected to higher female job satisfaction. That figure is therefore not quoted here. Dilmaghani's paper was read only in the abstract Wiley supplies through Crossref, the full text returning 403. Crosby's book of 1982 and Hodson's paper of 1989 were not read, and neither was the published 2019 Labour Economics version of the Vladisavljević and Perugini working paper. Nothing was found that measures workers' expectations directly. Clark's own account of the mechanism, as Vladisavljević and Perugini describe it, was indirect, resting on age, education and occupation as proxies that 'might be realistically correlated with expectations'.
misreadings: The name is the first trap. Herschbach's paper reports that the phenomenon 'has been called paradoxical' in two literatures at once, and that 'in medicine it is called the "satisfaction paradox" and in the social sciences the "well-being paradox"'. What is meant there is that objectively negative factors in a life have relatively little effect on subjective quality of life. That is a claim about illness, disability and hardship, and it is not the claim about women's jobs. Nothing on this page bears on it. The stronger version, that people in bad conditions are about as satisfied as anyone else, is contested for life satisfaction. Veenhoven writes that people are typically dissatisfied when they live in miserable conditions, that dissatisfaction is the rule in poor third world countries, and that in western nations life satisfaction is lower where adverse conditions accumulate. The disappearance of the British gap is read as a refutation of Clark, and it is closer to the opposite. He predicted that the paradox would be temporary, and Green and colleagues describe their result as roughly supporting that prediction. Nor was the pattern ever universal. In the 2013 EU-SILC data men were the more satisfied sex in several countries of eastern Europe. The finding is also used to argue that women's jobs are therefore acceptable. Clark's account says the reverse, that the satisfaction was a record of low expectations formed by a poor labour-market position.
